entries.17:4: They will lose the land God gave them and become slaves in a foreign country because their sin has stirred up God's anger like an unending fire. It means rejecting God can cost you what He gave you.
entries.17:5: God says a person is cursed who trusts in human beings and relies on their own strength instead of depending on Him. The reader is warned not to put ultimate trust in people or themselves.
entries.17:6: Such a person will be like a lonely shrub in the desert that never sees anything good come—living in a dry, salty wasteland. It pictures a life that dries up when it stops trusting God.
entries.17:7: God blesses the person who trusts in Him and puts their hope in Him. The reader is encouraged that trusting God brings real blessing.
entries.17:8: That person is like a tree planted by water with roots reaching the stream—it doesn't fear heat, stays green, and keeps bearing fruit even in drought. It means trusting God gives steady strength in hard times.
entries.17:9: The human heart is deceitful and crooked, and no person can fully understand it. The reader should be humble about their own motives and not assume they know their heart fully.
entries.17:10: God alone searches hearts and tests minds, and He rewards each person according to how they live. It means nothing is hidden from God, and He judges fairly.
entries.17:11: A man who gains wealth dishonestly is like a bird sitting on eggs that won't hatch—the wealth will leave him and he'll end up a fool. The reader is warned that ill-gotten gain doesn't last.
entries.17:12: God's glorious throne is exalted from the beginning, and His sanctuary is a place of honor. It reminds the reader that God is high and holy above all.
entries.17:13: Those who turn away from the Lord, the source of living water, will be shamed and cut off. The reader is warned that abandoning God means losing the source of true life.
entries.17:14: Jeremiah asks God to heal and save him, confessing that God is his hope. The reader can bring their need for healing and rescue to God with confidence.
entries.17:15: People mock Jeremiah, demanding that God's promised judgment actually happen. It shows how hard it is to be doubted when you speak God's truth.
entries.17:16: Jeremiah says he didn't wish disaster on his people and didn't want the day of death—and God knows everything he said. The reader sees an honest prophet who cared for people even while warning them.
entries.17:17: Jeremiah pleads with God not to become a source of terror to him, since God is his refuge in trouble. The reader can ask God to be their safe place when afraid.
entries.17:18: Jeremiah asks that his attackers be shamed and terrified instead of him, and that they be destroyed twice over. It shows a raw prayer for God to defend him against enemies.
entries.17:19: God tells Jeremiah to stand at the city gates where kings and people pass through. It means God's message was to be delivered publicly where everyone would hear it.
entries.17:20: Jeremiah is told to call the kings and all the people of Jerusalem to listen to God's word. The reader is reminded that God's message is for leaders and ordinary people alike.
entries.17:21: God warns the people to be careful not to carry loads or bring goods through Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath. It means they were to treat the Sabbath as special and not just another workday.
entries.17:22: They were not to carry loads from their houses or do any work on the Sabbath, but keep it holy as God commanded their ancestors. The reader learns that God takes rest and honor for Him seriously.
entries.17:23: Their ancestors paid no attention, stubbornly refused to listen, and wouldn't accept correction. It warns the reader against the same stubbornness toward God.
entries.17:24: God promises that if the people carefully obey and keep the Sabbath holy by not working, things will go well. It shows obedience brings blessing.
entries.17:25: If they obey, kings and princes will again ride through Jerusalem's gates with the people, and the city will stand forever. It means faithfulness to God secures a lasting future.
entries.17:26: People from all around Judah will come to God's house bringing sacrifices, incense, and thank offerings. It pictures restored worship and a community coming back to God.
entries.17:27: But if they refuse to keep the Sabbath holy, God will set an unquenchable fire in Jerusalem's gates that burns down its great houses. The reader is warned that ignoring God's clear commands brings serious judgment.
entries.18:1: God spoke directly to the prophet Jeremiah and gave him a message. It reminds the reader that God still speaks and wants people to listen.
entries.18:2: God told Jeremiah to go to a potter's workshop, promising to speak to him there. It shows God often teaches us through ordinary, everyday places and work.
entries.18:3: Jeremiah obeyed and found the potter working at his wheel. It simply shows the prophet going where God sent him and paying attention to what he saw.
entries.18:4: The clay pot the potter was shaping went wrong in his hands, so he reshaped it into a different pot as he chose. It shows that something spoiled can still be remade into something useful by the one in charge.
entries.18:5: God spoke to Jeremiah again after he had seen the potter at work. It shows God uses what we see to help us understand what he wants to say.
entries.18:6: God asked Israel whether he could not reshape them the way the potter reshapes clay, since they were like clay in his hands. It means God has the right and power to remake a people who have gone wrong.
entries.18:7: God says that whenever he announces he will tear down and destroy a nation, that warning is real. It means God is serious when he speaks about judgment.
entries.18:8: But if that nation turns from its evil, God says he will change his mind and not bring the disaster. It means it is never too late to turn around, because God responds to repentance.
entries.18:9: God also says that whenever he announces he will build up and plant a nation, that promise is real. It means God genuinely intends good for those he blesses.
entries.18:10: But if that nation does evil and disobeys, God says he will change his mind about the good he planned. It means God's blessings are not a guarantee if people turn away from him.
entries.18:11: God told Jeremiah to warn Judah and Jerusalem that he was planning disaster and to urge each person to turn from evil and change their ways. It means God warns people because he wants them to change, not because he wants to destroy them.
entries.18:12: The people answered that it was hopeless and that they would just follow their own stubborn desires. It shows how people can refuse help and choose to keep doing wrong even when warned.
entries.18:13: God told the nations to look and see how shocking Israel's behavior was, calling it something unheard of. It means God's people had done something so wrong that even outsiders would be stunned.
entries.18:14: God asked whether snow ever leaves the mountain peaks or cold mountain streams ever run dry. It means some things are steady and reliable, and his people's failure to be faithful stands out against that.
entries.18:15: God said his people had forgotten him and burned incense to worthless things, so he would make them stumble on their old paths and take them down unfamiliar, uneven roads. It means forgetting God leads people into confusion and trouble.
entries.18:16: God said their land would become a shocking sight that makes everyone who passes by gasp and shake their heads. It means the results of their choices would be visible and shameful to everyone.
entries.18:17: God said he would scatter them like wind before an enemy and turn away from them when disaster came. It means their rejection of God would leave them exposed and without his help.
entries.18:18: The people plotted against Jeremiah, saying they did not need his teaching and would attack him with his own words. It shows how people can reject a true message and turn on the one who brings it.
entries.18:19: Jeremiah asked God to pay attention to him and to listen to what his opponents were saying against him. It shows it is right to bring our troubles and unfair treatment to God in prayer.
entries.18:20: Jeremiah asked whether good should be repaid with evil, pointing out that he had pleaded with God to spare them from wrath. It means he felt hurt that people he had helped were now trying to trap him.
entries.18:21: Jeremiah asked God to bring severe judgment on his enemies, including famine, war, and loss for their families. It shows how deeply angry and hurt he was, and it is an honest cry for justice rather than a model for how we should pray about enemies.
entries.18:22: Jeremiah asked that cries of distress come from their homes when attackers strike suddenly, because they had set traps for him. It means he wanted God to see the harm they planned for him and to act.
entries.18:23: Jeremiah asked God not to forgive or overlook their plots against him but to deal with them in his anger. It shows he left vengeance in God's hands, though his request is raw and severe.
entries.19:1: God tells Jeremiah to buy a clay jar and bring along respected leaders and priests as witnesses. The reader should see that God sometimes asks his messenger to act out his message so people cannot miss it.
entries.19:2: Jeremiah is to take the jar to a specific valley near Jerusalem and announce there, loudly, the exact words God gives him. It means God's warnings are meant to be heard clearly, not whispered or softened.
entries.19:3: The leaders and people are told to listen because the God over all armies is announcing disaster on this place that will shock anyone who hears it. For the reader, ignoring God's word does not make his warnings go away.
entries.19:4: The disaster is coming because the people abandoned God, turned the place into a shrine for foreign gods they knew nothing about, and filled it with the blood of innocent people. It shows that treating God as unimportant and harming the innocent are serious in his eyes.
entries.19:5: They even built shrines to Baal and burned their own children as offerings, something God never commanded and never even considered. The reader learns that cruel acts done in the name of religion are not from God at all.
entries.19:6: Because of this, God says the place will be renamed from its old name to "the Valley of Death." It means sin changes a place and a people so deeply that their identity is marked by the harm they caused.
entries.19:7: God says he will let Judah's plans collapse there, and their enemies will kill them and leave their bodies for birds and wild animals. It is a sober picture that rejecting God's protection leaves people exposed to ruin.
entries.19:8: The city will become so devastated that passersby will gasp and mock at the sight of its troubles. For the reader, this is a warning that sin can bring public shame and destruction, not just private regret.
entries.19:9: The siege will become so desperate that people will eat their own children and each other because of starvation and enemy pressure. It shows how far human suffering can go when a society turns from God and faces the consequences.
entries.19:10: Jeremiah is told to smash the clay jar right in front of the leaders who came with him. The action makes the coming judgment visible and unforgettable to those watching.
entries.19:11: God says he will break this people and city like a smashed jar that can never be repaired, and the dead will fill the burial place until there is no room. It means some choices bring damage that cannot simply be undone.
entries.19:12: God declares he will make this city like the defiled valley of Topheth. The reader should understand that a place becomes what its people make it through their worship and choices.
entries.19:13: Even the houses of Jerusalem and of Judah's kings will be treated as unclean, because people burned incense and poured out drink offerings to the stars on their roofs. It shows that private and public worship of other gods contaminates ordinary life.
entries.19:14: Jeremiah leaves Topheth and stands in the temple courtyard to speak to all the people. It means God's message follows the people from the place of judgment back to the place of worship, so no one can claim they never heard.
entries.19:15: God says he will bring on the city and its surrounding towns all the disaster he promised, because the people stubbornly refused to listen to him. For the reader, refusing to listen to God is itself the reason judgment comes.
entries.20:1: Pashhur was the chief official in charge of the temple, and he heard what Jeremiah was preaching. This shows that Jeremiah's message reached people in power, who did not like what they heard.
entries.20:2: Pashhur had Jeremiah beaten and locked in wooden stocks at the temple gate. Jeremiah was punished for speaking God's message, which reminds us that telling the truth can cost us.
entries.20:3: The next day Pashhur released Jeremiah, and Jeremiah gave him a new name meaning 'terror on every side.' The name was a warning that fear and disaster were coming to Pashhur himself.
entries.20:4: God said Pashhur would become a source of fear to himself and his friends, and he would watch his friends die while Judah was taken captive to Babylon. The man who punished God's messenger would face the very judgment he denied.
entries.20:5: God said all the wealth and treasures of Jerusalem, including the king's stores, would be handed over to enemies who would carry them off to Babylon. The city's security and riches would not save it.
entries.20:6: Pashhur and everyone in his household would be taken captive to Babylon and die there, along with the friends he had misled with false words. His false teaching would end in exile and death for him and those who trusted him.
entries.20:7: Jeremiah complains that God overpowered and tricked him into being a prophet, and now everyone laughs at him. Even a faithful servant of God can feel betrayed and mocked when obedience brings only trouble.
entries.20:8: Every time Jeremiah speaks, he shouts about violence and destruction, and people mock God's word because of him. Speaking God's truth made him a target of ridicule all day long.
entries.20:9: Jeremiah tries to stop speaking for God, but the message burns inside him like a fire he cannot hold in. God's word is too strong to be silenced, even when speaking it hurts.
entries.20:10: People whisper threats about Jeremiah, and even his close friends watch for a chance to trip him up and get revenge. Being surrounded by secret enemies and false friends is a deep kind of loneliness.
entries.20:11: Jeremiah remembers that the Lord stands with him like a mighty warrior, so his attackers will stumble and fail. God's presence with him means his enemies will not have the last word.
entries.20:12: Jeremiah asks the Lord, who sees hearts and minds, to punish his persecutors because he has placed his case before God. It is right to bring our hurts to God and trust him to judge fairly.
entries.20:13: Jeremiah bursts into praise because the Lord rescues the poor and needy from those who do evil. Even in the middle of trouble, we can sing because God defends the helpless.
entries.20:14: Jeremiah curses the day he was born and wishes no blessing on it. His sorrow is so deep that he wishes he had never existed, showing how honest grief can be before God.
entries.20:15: Jeremiah curses the man who brought his father the happy news of his birth. The joy of that day now feels like a cruel joke to him in his pain.
entries.20:16: Jeremiah wishes that man would be destroyed like the cities God overthrew without mercy, hearing cries of distress from morning to noon. He wants his own suffering matched by judgment on the one who announced his birth.
entries.20:17: Jeremiah wishes he had been killed before birth, so his mother's womb would have been his grave forever. He is saying that death before birth would have been better than the life of pain he now endures.
entries.20:18: Jeremiah asks why he ever came out of the womb, only to see trouble and sorrow and spend his days in shame. His life feels like pointless suffering, and he pours out that complaint to God.
entries.21:1: This verse sets the scene: King Zedekiah sends two officials to ask the prophet Jeremiah a question. It shows that even a king turns to God's messenger when trouble comes.
entries.21:2: The officials ask Jeremiah to pray and find out what God says, hoping God will rescue them from the Babylonian army as he did in the past. It shows people wanting God's help only when they are in danger.
entries.21:3: Jeremiah agrees to answer, but the reply is not for the messengers alone; it is meant for the king himself. God's word here is directed at the person in charge.
entries.21:4: God says he will turn the city's own weapons against them and bring the enemy inside the walls. The defense they trusted will not save them.
entries.21:5: God says he himself will fight against his own people with great anger. This is a serious warning that sin can turn God's power against those who ignore him.
entries.21:6: God says disease will strike the people and animals in the city, causing many deaths. It shows how severe the judgment on the city will be.
entries.21:7: Those who survive disease, war, and hunger will be handed over to the Babylonian king with no mercy. It means no escape route remains for those who stay in their rebellion.
entries.21:8: God sets two clear choices before the people: a way that leads to life and a way that leads to death. Every person is faced with a choice about how to respond to God.
entries.21:9: Staying in the city means death by war, hunger, or disease, but surrendering to the Babylonians means survival. In this situation, the surprising path is the one that preserves life.
entries.21:10: God says he is set against this city to bring disaster, and it will be handed to Babylon and burned. It shows that God's judgment is certain when people refuse to turn back to him.
entries.21:11: This begins a message aimed specifically at the royal family of Judah. God's word comes to leaders with special attention because they carry responsibility for the people.
entries.21:12: God tells the king's family to do justice every day and rescue people who are being robbed or oppressed. If they don't, God's anger will burn and no one will be able to stop it.
entries.21:13: God speaks against those who feel secure on their high rocky position and think no enemy can reach them. It warns that no location or self-confidence can protect anyone from God.
entries.21:14: God says he will punish them for what they have done and set fire to everything around them. It means actions have consequences, and God holds people accountable for their deeds.
entries.22:1: God tells the prophet to go to the king's palace and deliver a message there. It means God speaks directly to those in power, and the reader should expect God to hold leaders accountable.
entries.22:2: The king, his officials, and everyone entering the palace are told to listen to God's word. It means no one is too important to hear God, and the reader should listen too.
entries.22:3: God commands fair judgment, rescuing the oppressed, and protecting foreigners, orphans, and widows from harm. It means God cares deeply about justice and the vulnerable, and the reader should treat people fairly and kindly.
entries.22:4: If the king obeys, his dynasty will continue with honor and security. It means obedience brings lasting good, and the reader should see that doing right has real rewards.
entries.22:5: If the king refuses to listen, God swears that the palace will be destroyed. It means ignoring God has serious consequences, and the reader should take God's warnings seriously.
entries.22:6: God compares the royal family to beautiful, lush places but says he will turn them into an empty wasteland. It means even something impressive can be brought down, and the reader should not trust in status or beauty.
entries.22:7: God will bring armed attackers who will cut down the palace's fine cedar wood and burn it. It means judgment will be thorough, and the reader should see that no luxury can protect against God's decision.
entries.22:8: People from other nations will pass by the ruined city and ask each other why God did this to such a great place. It means the downfall will be public and puzzling, and the reader should learn from others' mistakes.
entries.22:9: The answer will be that the people broke their agreement with God and worshiped other gods. It means abandoning God caused the disaster, and the reader should stay faithful to God.
entries.22:10: Don't mourn the dead king; mourn the one carried away, because he will never return home. It means exile is a deep loss, and the reader should value home and freedom.
entries.22:11: God says Shallum, who replaced his father Josiah as king, will never come back to this place. It means his rule is cut short, and the reader should see that power can be quickly taken away.
entries.22:12: He will die as a prisoner in a foreign land and never see his homeland again. It means his fate is sealed, and the reader should remember that choices lead to consequences.
entries.22:13: A curse is on anyone who builds a house by cheating others and not paying workers. It means God condemns unfair treatment of workers, and the reader should be honest and pay people fairly.
entries.22:14: The king boasts about building a huge house with fancy windows, cedar paneling, and red paint. It means he is obsessed with showing off wealth, and the reader should not chase luxury at others' expense.
entries.22:15: Being king isn't about having more cedar than your father; your father ate, drank, and did what was right, and things went well for him. It means good character matters more than fancy buildings, and the reader should focus on doing right.
entries.22:16: He defended the poor and needy, and that was good—that is what it means to know God. It means knowing God is shown by caring for the needy, and the reader should treat that as true faith.
entries.22:17: But this king only cares about his own profit, killing innocent people, and acting violently and cruelly. It means selfish greed leads to harm, and the reader should guard against putting profit above people.
entries.22:18: God says no one will mourn for Jehoiakim with cries of grief for a brother, sister, lord, or his glory. It means he will die unmourned, and the reader should see that a bad legacy leaves no real sorrow.
entries.22:19: He will be buried like a dead donkey—dragged out and thrown outside the city gates. It means he will be treated with disgrace, and the reader should see that dishonor follows cruelty.
entries.22:20: The people are told to cry out from the mountains because all their allies have been destroyed. It means their support is gone, and the reader should not rely on unreliable allies.
entries.22:21: God spoke to them when things were going well, but they refused to listen—that has been their habit since youth. It means ignoring God in good times leads to trouble, and the reader should listen now, not later.
entries.22:22: Their leaders will be blown away and their allies taken captive, and then they will be ashamed because of their evil. It means bad leadership and evil bring shame, and the reader should choose leaders and actions wisely.
entries.22:23: Those living comfortably in fine palaces will suffer sudden pain like a woman in childbirth. It means comfort can end abruptly, and the reader should not be smug about security.
entries.22:24: Even if the king were a signet ring on God's own hand, God would pull him off. It means no one is so special that God won't remove them, and the reader should stay humble.
entries.22:25: God will hand them over to those they fear—Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonians. It means running from fear doesn't help; God's judgment will find them, and the reader should trust God rather than fear.
entries.22:26: The king and his mother will be sent to a foreign land where they will die. It means exile will separate families, and the reader should value faithfulness that keeps families and homes secure.
entries.22:27: They will long to return to their homeland but will never get back. It means longing without repentance doesn't restore what was lost, and the reader should turn to God before it's too late.
entries.22:28: The prophet asks if this man is a broken, worthless pot that gets thrown out with his children into a strange land. It means the king's line is rejected, and the reader should see that unfaithfulness makes people useless for God's purposes.
entries.22:29: The earth itself is called to listen to God's word. It means the message is serious and universal, and the reader should pay attention as something that matters to all creation.
entries.22:30: God says this man will be recorded as childless, with no descendant to rule on David's throne. It means his family line loses the kingship, and the reader should see that disobedience can end a legacy.
entries.23:1: God pronounces judgment on the leaders who were supposed to care for His people but instead caused them harm and loss. It reminds readers that those entrusted with caring for others are accountable to God for how they treat them.
entries.23:2: God directly confronts the leaders for scattering His people and neglecting them, and He promises to punish them for this failure. It means neglect and mistreatment of those under your care does not go unnoticed by God.
entries.23:3: God promises to gather the scattered remnant of His people from every place they were driven and bring them back home, where they will thrive and grow. It shows that even after failure and exile, God works to restore and multiply His people.
entries.23:4: God promises to appoint faithful leaders who will genuinely care for His people, so they will no longer live in fear or be troubled, and none will be lost. It gives hope that God Himself ensures His people are protected and well-shepherded.
entries.23:5: God announces a coming day when He will raise up a righteous descendant of David who will rule with wisdom, justice, and integrity. It points to a future faithful king—ultimately fulfilled in Christ—who governs rightly.
entries.23:6: In that coming king's reign, God's people will be saved and live securely, and He will be known as the One who provides righteousness. It means safety and right standing with God come through this promised ruler.
entries.23:7: A future day is coming when people will no longer refer to God primarily by the exodus from Egypt. It signals that God will do something so great it becomes the new defining act of His faithfulness.
entries.23:8: Instead, people will speak of God as the One who brought His people back from the northern lands and all the places of exile, and they will live in their own land. It means God's future rescue will be so remarkable it surpasses even the memory of Egypt.
entries.23:9: The prophet Jeremiah describes his own deep anguish—his heart broken and his body trembling—because of the Lord's words against the false prophets. It shows that speaking God's truth can be emotionally devastating, even for the one delivering it.
entries.23:10: The land is filled with adultery and evil, and because of this the land mourns and even the wilderness pastures dry up; people use their strength for wrongdoing. It means widespread moral corruption has real consequences for the whole community and the land itself.
entries.23:11: Both prophets and priests have become corrupt, and God has seen their wickedness even in His own house. It warns that religious leaders are not exempt from judgment when they practice evil.
entries.23:12: Because of their corruption, their path will become slippery; they will be driven into darkness and fall, and God will bring disaster on them in the appointed time of punishment. It means sin leads to a downfall that cannot be avoided.
entries.23:13: God points out the foolishness of the prophets of Samaria, who prophesied by Baal and led His people Israel astray. It shows that leading people away from God is a serious offense, even when done sincerely.
entries.23:14: Among the prophets of Jerusalem God sees shocking things—adultery, deceit, and strengthening evildoers so they don't turn from their wickedness; they have become as corrupt as Sodom and Gomorrah. It means leaders who make evil easier rather than calling people to repent are deeply offensive to God.
entries.23:15: God declares that He will feed these prophets bitter food and give them bitter water to drink, because their corrupt behavior has spread throughout the land. It means the consequences of their sin will be bitter and unavoidable.
entries.23:16: God warns His people not to listen to these prophets, whose visions come from their own minds rather than from the mouth of the Lord. It means not every claim to speak for God is genuine, and we must test what we hear.
entries.23:17: These false prophets keep telling those who reject God's word that they will have peace, and telling the proud that no harm will come to them. It means false comfort that ignores sin is dangerous and deceptive.
entries.23:18: God asks which of these prophets has actually stood in His council, seen Him, and truly listened to His word. It means genuine prophetic authority comes from actually hearing God, not from claiming to.
entries.23:19: God's anger is described as a storm wind that has gone out and will burst on the heads of evildoers. It means God's judgment is real and will come with unstoppable force.
entries.23:20: God's anger will not relent until He has accomplished everything He intends, and in the future His people will fully understand this. It means God's purposes will be completed, even if we don't understand them now.
entries.23:21: God says He did not send these prophets, yet they ran anyway; He did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. It means self-appointed messengers who speak without God's commission are not truly from Him.
entries.23:22: If these prophets had truly stood in God's council, they would have called His people to turn from their evil ways. It means the mark of a true messenger is that their words lead people away from sin.
entries.23:23: God asks whether He is only a God who is near and not also a God far away. It means God is not limited to one place or one situation—He is present everywhere.
entries.23:24: God asks whether anyone can hide in a secret place where He cannot see them, and whether there is any place in heaven or earth where He is not. It means nothing is hidden from God, and no one can escape His presence.
entries.23:25: God says He has heard the false prophets who keep saying they have had dreams in His name. It means claiming divine revelation for something God never said is something God takes seriously.
entries.23:26: God questions how long this will go on—whether His word is really in the hearts of prophets who speak lies from their own deceitful hearts. It means a heart full of deception cannot genuinely carry God's truth.
entries.23:27: These prophets intend to make God's people forget His name through their dreams, just as their ancestors forgot Him for Baal. It means false teaching can gradually erode people's loyalty to God.
entries.23:28: A prophet with a dream should tell it as a dream, but the one who has God's word should speak it faithfully; straw has nothing to do with grain. It means God's true word is fundamentally different from human speculation and should not be mixed with it.
entries.23:29: God describes His word as fire and as a hammer that shatters rock. It means God's word is powerful—it burns away falsehood and breaks down hardness.
entries.23:30: God declares Himself against the prophets who steal words from one another. It means those who merely copy or borrow messages rather than receiving them from God are opposed by Him.
entries.23:31: God is against the prophets who use their tongues to declare, 'He has said,' when God has not spoken. It means putting words in God's mouth is a serious offense.
entries.23:32: God is against those who prophesy false dreams, deceive people with their reckless words, and lead His people astray—though He never sent them or commanded them, and they will not benefit the people. It means ministries not sent by God ultimately help no one.
entries.23:33: If people, prophets, or priests ask what burden or message comes from the Lord, God tells Jeremiah to answer that they themselves are the burden, and He will cast them off. It means treating God's word lightly turns the message against the messenger.
entries.23:34: Anyone—prophet, priest, or layperson—who claims to have a burden from the Lord will be punished along with their household. It means misusing God's name brings judgment on the person and their family.
entries.23:35: Instead of using the phrase 'burden of the Lord,' people should simply ask one another what answer or word the Lord has given. It means we should speak about God's word plainly and honestly, not as a slogan.
entries.23:36: God says people must stop using the phrase 'burden of the Lord,' because each person's own words will become their burden, and they have twisted the words of the living God. It means careless misuse of God's words turns back on the one who misuses them.
entries.23:37: God instructs Jeremiah to ask the prophet directly what answer the Lord has given and what the Lord has said. It means we should press for the actual content of God's word, not just religious language.
entries.23:38: If people insist on saying 'the burden of the Lord,' God says that because they use this phrase despite His command not to, He will hold them accountable. It means deliberately disobeying God's instruction about how to speak of Him brings consequences.
entries.23:39: Because of this, God says He will completely forget them and cast them and the city He gave to them and their ancestors out of His presence. It means persistent rejection of God's word leads to being cut off from Him and from blessing.
entries.23:40: God will give them an everlasting disgrace and an unending shame that will never be forgotten. It means the dishonor that comes from rejecting God's word is permanent and public.
entries.24:1: Jeremiah sees a vision of two baskets of figs placed at the Temple, right after Babylon's king had taken Judah's king and many skilled people away as captives. It sets the scene: God is about to explain what those two groups of people mean.
entries.24:2: One basket held fresh, good figs that ripen early, and the other held figs so rotten they couldn't be eaten. The two baskets stand for two very different groups of people.
entries.24:3: God asks Jeremiah what he sees, and Jeremiah answers honestly that the good figs are very good and the bad ones are too rotten to eat. God uses simple, everyday pictures to teach a serious lesson.
entries.24:4: This short line simply marks that God is now speaking directly to Jeremiah. What follows is God's own explanation of the vision.
entries.24:5: God says the people already taken away to Babylon are like the good figs, and he means it for their good. Even being carried off to a foreign land does not mean God has abandoned them.
entries.24:6: God promises to watch over those exiles kindly, bring them home, and rebuild them rather than tear them down. Their hard season has a hopeful ending because God is still caring for them.
entries.24:7: God promises to give them a heart that truly knows him, so they will be his people and he will be their God. They will return to him wholeheartedly, which is the deepest good anyone can receive.
entries.24:8: God says the people still left in Jerusalem and those who fled to Egypt are like the rotten figs, and he names King Zedekiah and his officials. Staying put or running to Egypt would not save them from what was coming.
entries.24:9: Those people will become a warning and a byword among the nations, a source of fear, shame, and mocking wherever they are scattered. Their downfall will be talked about everywhere as an example.
entries.24:10: God will send war, hunger, and disease against them until they are gone from the land he gave their ancestors. This is a sober warning that ignoring God's word has real and serious consequences.
entries.25:1: This verse dates Jeremiah's message to a specific year, tying his words to real events in history. It shows that God's warnings came at an actual moment in time, not as vague stories.
entries.25:2: Jeremiah spoke this message openly to everyone in Judah and Jerusalem. The point is that God's warning was not hidden—it was announced publicly to all the people.
entries.25:3: For twenty-three years Jeremiah kept delivering God's word to the people, but they refused to listen. It shows God's patience in warning people again and again, and the sad result when they ignore Him.
entries.25:4: God kept sending prophet after prophet to the people, but they paid no attention. This means God does not give up easily, yet ignoring His messengers has consequences.
entries.25:5: The message was simple: turn from evil and you can stay in the land God gave you. It means God offers a real way back, and turning from wrong doing is what keeps us in His blessing.
entries.25:6: God warned them not to chase after other gods, because doing so would only hurt themselves. It means our wrong choices don't damage God—they damage us.
entries.25:7: The people refused to listen and made God angry by what they did, which brought harm on themselves. It means ignoring God's warnings ends up costing us, not Him.
entries.25:8: Because the people would not listen to God's words, judgment was now coming. It means refusing to hear God's voice has real results.
entries.25:9: God says He will use Babylon and its king to bring judgment on Judah and the surrounding nations. It means even powerful enemies are under God's control, and He can use them to carry out His purposes.
entries.25:10: The joy of everyday life—laughter, weddings, work, and light—will be taken away. It means judgment strips away the ordinary joys we take for granted.
entries.25:11: The land will be ruined and the nations will serve Babylon for seventy years. It means God sets a limit on hard times; they do not last forever.
entries.25:12: After seventy years, God will punish Babylon for its own evil and ruin it too. It means no oppressor escapes forever—God holds even the powerful accountable.
entries.25:13: God will bring on Babylon everything He warned about through Jeremiah. It means God's words are reliable—what He says will happen, happens.
entries.25:14: Many nations and great kings will make Babylon serve them, and Babylon will get back what it did to others. It means cruelty comes back on those who practice it.
entries.25:15: God tells Jeremiah to take a cup of His anger and make the nations drink it. It pictures God's judgment being poured out, and no nation is exempt.
entries.25:16: Those who drink will stagger and lose their senses because of the violence coming on them. It means God's judgment leaves people helpless and confused.
entries.25:17: Jeremiah did what God said and gave the cup to all the nations God sent him to. It means the prophet faithfully delivered God's message, even when it was hard.
entries.25:18: Judah and Jerusalem were first to drink, becoming a ruin and a warning to others. It means God judges His own people first, not just outsiders.
entries.25:19: Egypt and its leaders were included in the judgment. It means no nation, however strong, is outside God's reach.
entries.25:20: A long list of peoples and Philistine cities are named as receiving judgment. It means God's justice covers every group and place, not just the obvious ones.
entries.25:21: Edom, Moab, and Ammon are named next. It means neighboring nations who opposed God's people are also accountable to Him.
entries.25:22: Tyre, Sidon, and lands across the sea are included. It means even distant places and trading powers fall under God's judgment.
entries.25:23: Desert peoples and tribes with distinctive customs are named. It means God sees and judges every people group, even remote ones.
entries.25:24: The kings of Arabia and desert peoples are included. It means no region or culture is overlooked by God.
entries.25:25: Elam, Media, and other kingdoms are named. It means powerful empires of the day are still answerable to God.
entries.25:26: All the kingdoms of the world, near and far, are included in the cup of judgment. It means God's judgment is universal—every kingdom on earth is accountable to Him.
entries.25:27: The nations are told to drink, stagger, fall, and not rise again because of the sword coming on them. It means God's judgment is severe and leaves no easy recovery.
entries.25:28: If a nation refuses to drink the cup, they are told they will still have to. It means no one can opt out of God's judgment by refusing to acknowledge it.
entries.25:29: God begins judgment with the city that bears His name, so no one else should expect to escape. It means if God's own people are judged, everyone else should take it seriously.
entries.25:30: God will roar like a lion from His holy place against all the earth. It means God is not silent—He speaks powerfully and everyone will hear it.
entries.25:31: The noise of God's case against the nations reaches the ends of the earth, and He judges all people. It means God has a rightful complaint against evil and will settle it.
entries.25:32: Evil spreads from nation to nation like a great storm rising from the earth. It means trouble and conflict move across the world, but God is still over it.
entries.25:33: The dead will lie unburied from one end of the earth to the other, with no one to mourn them. It means the results of judgment are grim and total, a serious warning.
entries.25:34: Leaders are told to weep and roll in dust because their destruction has come. It means those in charge are not shielded—they will answer for their leadership.
entries.25:35: The shepherds and leaders will have no escape route. It means when judgment comes, no clever plan or position can save those who ignored God.
entries.25:36: The leaders cry out bitterly because God has ruined their peaceful fields. It means the security people trusted in can be stripped away.
entries.25:37: The peaceful fields are silent because of God's burning anger. It means sin brings loss of peace, and God's anger is real, not imaginary.
entries.25:38: God is pictured as a lion leaving its hiding place, and the land is ruined by the sword and His anger. It means God will act, and His judgment is as serious as a lion on the hunt.
entries.26:1: God gave Jeremiah a message at the start of a new king's reign in Judah. It reminds us that God speaks into real moments in history, including the times we live in.
entries.26:2: God told Jeremiah to stand in the temple courtyard and tell the worshippers everything God commanded, holding nothing back. It means we should share God's message honestly and completely, not just the parts people like.
entries.26:3: God hoped the people would listen and turn from their wrong ways, so he could hold back the disaster he had planned. It shows God's mercy: he gives people a chance to change before judgment comes.
entries.26:4: God warned that if the people refused to listen and follow his law, there would be consequences. It means ignoring what God has clearly said is a serious choice with real results.
entries.26:5: God reminded them he had sent prophets again and again, but the people paid no attention. It means God keeps reaching out to us patiently, and we shouldn't keep ignoring him.
entries.26:6: God said he would make the temple like Shiloh, an old worship site that was destroyed, and make the city a byword among nations. It means no special building or status can protect us if we refuse to obey God.
entries.26:7: Jeremiah spoke these words publicly in the temple while the priests, prophets, and people listened. It shows that speaking God's truth openly can put us in front of people who won't like it.
entries.26:8: As soon as Jeremiah finished, the religious leaders and the crowd seized him and threatened to kill him. It means doing what God says can bring strong opposition, even from religious people.
entries.26:9: The crowd demanded to know why Jeremiah had prophesied that the temple and land would be ruined, and they gathered against him. It shows how angry people get when someone challenges what they trust in.
entries.26:10: When the officials heard what was happening, they came from the palace and sat at the temple gate to judge the case. It means there are times when authorities step in to keep a situation from turning violent.
entries.26:11: The priests and prophets told the officials and the crowd that Jeremiah deserved to die for speaking against the city. It shows how people can twist a true message from God into a charge of treason.
entries.26:12: Jeremiah calmly told the officials and the people that God had sent him to speak those very words against the temple and city. It means we can stand firm and honest when we know we're doing what God sent us to do.
entries.26:13: Jeremiah urged them to change their ways and listen to God, and said God would then hold back the disaster. It means it's never too late to turn around and receive God's mercy.
entries.26:14: Jeremiah put himself in their hands, saying they could do with him whatever seemed right to them. It shows real courage and trust in God when we leave the outcome to others and to God.
entries.26:15: Jeremiah warned that killing an innocent man would make them and their city guilty of shedding innocent blood, because God really had sent him. It means harming someone who speaks God's truth brings guilt on those who do it.
entries.26:16: The officials and the people decided Jeremiah should not die, since he had spoken to them in the name of the Lord their God. It shows that fair-minded people can recognize a true message even when it's uncomfortable.
entries.26:17: Some of the respected elders of the land stood up and addressed the whole assembly. It means wise, experienced voices can calm a dangerous situation and bring perspective.
entries.26:18: The elders recalled that the prophet Micah had once predicted Zion would be plowed like a field and the temple mount become wooded heights. It shows that hard warnings from God's prophets have happened before and were taken seriously.
entries.26:19: The elders pointed out that King Hezekiah did not kill Micah; instead he feared the Lord and prayed, and God held back the disaster. It means responding to God's warning with repentance saves us from bringing harm on ourselves.
entries.26:20: Another prophet, Uriah, had also spoken the same warnings from God against the city and land. It shows that Jeremiah was not alone; others had delivered the same message and faced danger.
entries.26:21: When King Jehoiakim and his soldiers heard Uriah's words, the king wanted to kill him, so Uriah fled in fear to Egypt. It means fear can make us run, but running doesn't always keep us safe from powerful people.
entries.26:22: King Jehoiakim sent Elnathan and some men to Egypt to go after Uriah. It shows how far a hostile ruler will go to silence someone who speaks God's truth.
entries.26:23: They brought Uriah back from Egypt, and the king had him killed and buried with the common people. It's a sober reminder that faithfulness to God can cost everything, and that evil rulers can do terrible things.
entries.26:24: Ahikam son of Shaphan protected Jeremiah, so he was not handed over to the crowd to be killed. It means one person's courage and support can make the difference between life and death for someone doing God's work.
entries.27:1: God gave Jeremiah a message at the time Zedekiah became king of Judah. It shows God still spoke to his people through a prophet even during a time of political change.
entries.27:2: God told Jeremiah to make a wooden yoke, like the kind used on oxen, and wear it on his neck. It was a visual sign to show that a heavy burden of servitude was coming.
entries.27:3: Jeremiah was to send messages through the envoys of several neighboring kings who had come to Jerusalem. God's warning was not just for Judah but for the surrounding nations too.
entries.27:4: The envoys were to carry God's message back to their own kings. God wanted these rulers to hear his word directly and know what he was about to do.
entries.27:5: God says he made the whole earth and everything in it by his own power. Because he made it all, he has the right to give authority over it to whomever he chooses.
entries.27:6: God says he has handed the lands to Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, calling him his servant. Even a foreign king was being used by God to carry out his plan.
entries.27:7: All these nations will serve Babylon's king, then his son, then his grandson, for a set time. After that, Babylon itself will be conquered by other nations and kings.
entries.27:8: Any nation that refuses to serve Babylon will face war, famine, and disease from God. Resistance to what God has decided would only bring greater suffering.
entries.27:9: The people must not listen to their prophets, fortune-tellers, dream interpreters, or sorcerers. These voices were telling them they would not have to serve Babylon, which was not true.
entries.27:10: Those false prophets were lying to the people. Following their advice would lead to being driven from the land and destroyed.
entries.27:11: God promises that any nation willing to serve Babylon will be allowed to stay in its own land. Submission, though humbling, would mean survival and peace.
entries.27:12: Jeremiah gave the same message to King Zedekiah of Judah. He urged him to accept Babylon's rule so that he and his people would live.
entries.27:13: Jeremiah asks why the king and people would choose death through war, famine, and disease. Refusing Babylon's rule would bring the very disaster God warned about.
entries.27:14: The prophets claiming they would not serve Babylon were not to be trusted. Their message was a lie, no matter how confident they sounded.
entries.27:15: God says he did not send those prophets; they were speaking lies in his name. Their false message would only bring destruction on themselves and on those who listened.
entries.27:16: Jeremiah told the priests and people not to believe prophets who said the temple treasures would soon return from Babylon. That promise was false.
entries.27:17: Jeremiah urged the people not to listen to those prophets but to serve Babylon and live. Otherwise the city itself would be left in ruins.
entries.27:18: If those men really were prophets, they should pray to God that the remaining temple treasures would not be carried off to Babylon. A true prophet would intercede, not just make confident claims.
entries.27:19: God had more to say about the valuable items still left in the city. These were the things not yet taken away.
entries.27:20: These were the items Nebuchadnezzar left behind when he took King Jeconiah and Judah's leading men captive to Babylon. The earlier exile had not emptied the temple completely.
entries.27:21: God, the commander of heavenly armies and Israel's God, spoke specifically about those remaining treasures. His word was directed at what was still in the temple, the palace, and Jerusalem.
entries.27:22: God said those remaining treasures would also be taken to Babylon and stay there until he acted. But he promised a day when he would bring them back to their rightful place.
entries.28:1: A false prophet named Hananiah publicly confronted Jeremiah in the temple during King Zedekiah's reign, claiming to speak for God. It shows that not everyone who claims to speak for God is telling the truth, so we should weigh what we hear.
entries.28:2: Hananiah announced that God had broken Babylon's power over Judah, which sounded like good news but was not from God. A message can be comforting and still be false, so pleasant words alone don't prove God said them.
entries.28:3: Hananiah promised that within two years the temple treasures taken to Babylon would be returned. He was offering a hopeful prediction that God had not actually made.
entries.28:4: Hananiah also claimed the exiled king and all the captives would come home soon because Babylon's grip would be broken. This contradicted what God had truly said through Jeremiah.
entries.28:5: Jeremiah answered Hananiah openly in front of the priests and the crowd at the temple. He was willing to respond to a public claim publicly.
entries.28:6: Jeremiah said he wished Hananiah's prediction were true and that God would indeed bring the treasures and exiles back. Wanting peace doesn't mean we should pretend a false message is from God.
entries.28:7: Jeremiah asked the people to listen carefully to what he was about to say. He wanted them to think rather than just accept the popular message.
entries.28:8: Jeremiah pointed out that prophets long before them usually warned of war, disaster, and disease, not just good news. God's true messengers often say hard things, not only what people want to hear.
entries.28:9: A prophet who promises peace is only proven true when it actually happens. Claims about the future should be tested by whether they come true.
entries.28:10: Hananiah grabbed the wooden yoke Jeremiah was wearing and smashed it in front of everyone. He was acting out his false message with a dramatic gesture.
entries.28:11: Hananiah declared that God would break Babylon's yoke off all the nations within two years, and Jeremiah simply walked away. Sometimes the wisest response to a false claim is to leave it for God to settle.
entries.28:12: After Hananiah broke the yoke, God gave Jeremiah a new message. God was not silent about the false prophecy.
entries.28:13: God told Jeremiah to tell Hananiah that breaking a wooden yoke was easy, but the result would be an iron yoke that could not be broken. Resisting God's plan makes the burden heavier, not lighter.
entries.28:14: God declared that all these nations, including Judah, would truly serve Nebuchadnezzar, and even the wild animals would be under his control. God's purposes stand even when people deny them.
entries.28:15: Jeremiah told Hananiah plainly that God had not sent him and that he was leading the people to trust a lie. Teachers who claim God's authority without it do real harm to those who believe them.
entries.28:16: God said Hananiah would die that very year because he had spoken rebellion against the Lord. Speaking falsely in God's name is serious, not a small matter.
entries.28:17: Hananiah died two months later, exactly as God had said. The event confirmed that Jeremiah spoke for God and that God's word comes true.
entries.29:1: Jeremiah wrote a letter from Jerusalem to the Jewish leaders and people who had been taken captive to Babylon. It shows that God still cared about his people even far from home.
entries.29:2: This notes that the king, the queen mother, officials, and skilled workers had already been deported to Babylon. The letter was meant for people who had lost their homeland and normal life.
entries.29:3: The letter was carried by two messengers sent by King Zedekiah to the king of Babylon. It reminds us that God's message reached his people through ordinary travel and politics.
entries.29:4: God himself is speaking to the exiles, calling them people he had allowed to be taken to Babylon. He wants them to know he is still in charge of their situation.
entries.29:5: God tells the exiles to settle down, build homes, and plant gardens. Instead of just waiting to leave, they should live normal, productive lives where they are.
entries.29:6: They are told to marry and raise families, growing in number rather than shrinking. God wants his people to keep living and thriving even in a foreign land.
entries.29:7: They should work for the good of the city where they live and pray for it, because its well-being is tied to their own. God cares about the place where his people are, not just their eventual return.
entries.29:8: God warns them not to be fooled by false prophets or fortune-tellers among them, or by dreams they claim are from God. Not everyone who claims to speak for God is telling the truth.
entries.29:9: Those prophets are speaking lies in God's name, and God says he did not send them. We should test claims about God rather than accept them just because someone sounds religious.
entries.29:10: God promises that after seventy years in Babylon he will keep his good plan and bring them back home. Even a long wait does not cancel God's promises.
entries.29:11: God's plan for his people is good, even while they wait in a hard season. A plan can be real before it is visible.
entries.29:12: God says they will call on him and pray, and he will listen. Prayer is not wasted; God pays attention to people who cry out to him.
entries.29:13: If they look for God with their whole heart, they will find him. God is found by those who seek him sincerely, not half-heartedly.
entries.29:14: God promises to be found by them, restore their fortunes, and gather them back from everywhere they were scattered. No distance or exile is too far for God to bring his people home.
entries.29:15: The people were pointing to prophets in Babylon as proof things were fine. God is about to correct that false confidence.
entries.29:16: God now speaks about the king still ruling in Jerusalem and the people who were not taken captive. He has not forgotten those left behind either.
entries.29:17: God says he will bring war, famine, and disease on them and make them like rotten figs too bad to eat. Judgment is coming on those who ignored him.
entries.29:18: God will pursue them with war, hunger, and disease and make them a shocking warning among the nations. Their refusal to listen will have serious consequences.
entries.29:19: The reason is that they would not listen to God's words sent through his prophets, who kept reaching out to them. Ignoring God's repeated warnings brings its own result.
entries.29:20: God now addresses the exiles directly, calling them to listen carefully to his word. Even in exile, they are still his people and still accountable to him.
entries.29:21: God names two false prophets, Ahab and Zedekiah, who lied in his name, and says the king of Babylon will put them to death publicly. False teaching carries real danger.
entries.29:22: The exiles will use these two men's names as a curse, saying may God make you like them. Their shameful end will become a warning story.
entries.29:23: They did shameful things in Israel, committed adultery with neighbors' wives, and spoke lies in God's name without being sent. God sees such hidden sins and testifies against them.
entries.29:24: This introduces Shemaiah, a man from Nehelam, whose actions God is about to address. The passage turns to another false voice opposing Jeremiah.
entries.29:25: Shemaiah sent letters in his own name to Zephaniah the priest and others in Jerusalem. He was stirring up opposition by letter.
entries.29:26: Shemaiah claims Zephaniah has authority to arrest anyone acting like a crazy prophet and put them in prison. He is using religious authority to silence God's true messenger.
entries.29:27: Shemaiah asks why Zephaniah has not stopped Jeremiah from prophesying to them. He wants the true prophet punished, not heard.
entries.29:28: Shemaiah complains that Jeremiah told the exiles the captivity would last a long time and they should settle down. He resents a message that contradicts his own claims.
entries.29:29: Zephaniah the priest read Shemaiah's letter to Jeremiah so he knew what was being said. God's prophet was kept informed of the opposition against him.
entries.29:30: Then God gave Jeremiah a new message. God responds to those who attack his true messengers.
entries.29:31: God tells Jeremiah to send word to all the exiles that Shemaiah prophesied without being sent and led them to trust lies. False teachers mislead the people who follow them.
entries.29:32: God says he will punish Shemaiah and his family; none of them will see the good God will do for his people, because he spoke against the Lord. Speaking against God and leading others astray has serious consequences.
entries.30:1: God gave Jeremiah a message to deliver. It reminds us that what follows is not human opinion but words God wanted spoken.
entries.30:2: God told Jeremiah to write his words down in a book so they would be kept. Writing them down means later generations could read and remember what God had promised.
entries.30:3: God promised that a time was coming when he would bring his people back from exile to the land he had given their ancestors. Even after long hardship, God planned to restore them.
entries.30:4: This verse simply introduces the message that follows, showing it applies to both Israel and Judah. God's words here are meant for his whole divided people.
entries.30:5: The people were hearing sounds of panic and terror instead of peace. It describes how frightening their situation had become.
entries.30:6: Jeremiah asks whether men can give birth, then points out that strong men are doubled over in pain like women in labor. The picture shows that the suffering was severe and unusual, affecting everyone.
entries.30:7: This describes a time of terrible trouble for God's people, worse than any other. Yet the verse ends with hope: they will be rescued from it.
entries.30:8: God promised to break the heavy yoke and chains of slavery off his people's necks. Foreign nations would no longer be able to force them into service.
entries.30:9: Instead of serving foreign masters, the people would serve the Lord their God and a king from David's line. God would give them back proper leadership under him.
entries.30:10: God tells his people not to be afraid, because he will bring them home from distant lands and captivity. They will return to quiet and safety, with no one to frighten them.
entries.30:11: God promises to be with his people and save them, and he will not let them be completely destroyed. He will discipline them fairly, like a loving parent correcting a child, not wipe them out.
entries.30:12: God says the people's injury is serious and their wound is painful. Their condition is bad, and it is not something they can easily fix themselves.
entries.30:13: No one is coming to help their wound or offer a cure. They are left without human help, which makes their need for God clear.
entries.30:14: The allies they trusted have forgotten them and stopped caring. God says he himself allowed this painful blow because of their wrongdoing, so they would turn back to him.
entries.30:15: God asks why they keep crying over their wound when their guilt is so great. Their pain is real, but it came because of their own serious sins.
entries.30:16: God promises to turn the tables on those who hurt and plunder his people. The attackers and destroyers will themselves be attacked and destroyed.
entries.30:17: God promises to heal his people and mend their wounds. He does this partly because others had written them off as abandoned and worthless.
entries.30:18: God promises to restore the homes and towns of his people and show them mercy. Ruined places will be rebuilt and lived in again.
entries.30:19: Thanksgiving and laughter will come from the restored people. God will make them numerous and honored again, not small and weak.
entries.30:20: Their children will be secure as in earlier good times, and the community will be established before God. He will punish anyone who oppresses them.
entries.30:21: Their leader will be one of their own people, not a foreigner, and will be allowed to come near to God. This points to close relationship with God being restored.
entries.30:22: God restates the heart of the covenant: they will belong to him and he will be their God. This is the goal of all the restoration he promised.
entries.30:23: God's anger is pictured as a violent storm sweeping down on those who do evil. It shows that God takes wrongdoing seriously and acts against it.
entries.30:24: God's anger will not stop until he has fully carried out his purposes. Later, people will understand clearly what God was doing all along.
entries.31:1: God promises that a day is coming when he will be close to every family of Israel and they will belong to him. For the reader, it means God's commitment to his people is personal and complete, not distant.
entries.31:2: God reminds Israel that even when they went through a barren, dangerous wilderness, they found grace and safety, and he brought them to a place of rest. It means God stays with his people through hard seasons and leads them to peace.
entries.31:3: God says his love for his people has always been and always will be, and that love is what drew them to himself. For the reader, it means you are loved with a lasting love, not a temporary feeling.
entries.31:4: God promises to rebuild Israel and bring back music and dancing. It means mourning will turn into celebration, and joy will return after ruin.
entries.31:5: God promises that vineyards will be planted again in Samaria and people will actually enjoy the fruit. It means ordinary life and work will be restored, not just survival.
entries.31:6: A day is coming when people in the northern hills will call each other to go up to worship God in Zion. It means worship and community will be revived and people will eagerly seek God together.
entries.31:7: God tells his people to sing and shout the news that he has saved them. It means salvation is worth celebrating out loud and sharing with others.
entries.31:8: God promises to bring his scattered people home from far away, including the blind, the lame, and pregnant women, a huge crowd. It means no one is too weak or too far off for God to bring back.
entries.31:9: They will come home weeping, but God will lead them like a father along a safe path beside water. It means God guides his people tenderly, even when their return is emotional and messy.
entries.31:10: God tells the nations to spread the news that he will gather his scattered people and care for them like a shepherd. It means God's care is reliable and worth telling the whole world about.
entries.31:11: God has paid the price to set his people free from a power stronger than they were. It means God rescues people who cannot rescue themselves.
entries.31:12: The people will come singing to God's good gifts, and their lives will be like a well-watered garden with no more sorrow. It means God's provision brings deep, lasting joy instead of grief.
entries.31:13: God promises to turn weeping into joy, and young and old alike will dance and be glad. It means sorrow is not the end of the story; God brings comfort and gladness.
entries.31:14: God promises to satisfy the priests and fill his people with his good things. It means God's generosity is abundant and reaches everyone who serves and follows him.
entries.31:15: A voice of bitter weeping is heard in Ramah, Rachel crying for her children and refusing comfort. It means real grief is acknowledged, not brushed aside, even in the middle of God's promises.
entries.31:16: God tells the mourners to stop crying because their work will be rewarded and their people will return from the enemy's land. It means your labor and tears are not wasted; God will bring a return.
entries.31:17: God promises hope for the future and that children will come back to their own land. It means the future is not closed off; God is working toward restoration.
entries.31:18: Ephraim admits it was disciplined like an untrained calf and asks God to bring it back. It means it is honest and good to admit you need God to change you.
entries.31:19: After turning back, the people feel deep regret and shame over their earlier ways. It means real repentance includes sorrow over the past, and that sorrow is part of healing.
entries.31:20: God calls Ephraim his dear son and says his heart is troubled for him, so he will surely show mercy. It means God's discipline does not cancel his love; he still longs to be merciful.
entries.31:21: God tells his people to set up road markers and return by the way they left. It means it is possible to come back home, and it helps to remember the road you took.
entries.31:22: God asks how long his people will wander and says he is doing something new on the earth. It means God can do something surprising and fresh to end aimless drifting.
entries.31:23: God promises that when he restores Judah, people will again speak blessings over its towns and holy mountain. It means ordinary places will be filled with blessing and right living again.
entries.31:24: Judah and all its towns will live there together, farmers and shepherds alike. It means restored community includes everyday work and ordinary people living side by side.
entries.31:25: God promises to refresh the tired and give full strength to every sorrowing soul. It means exhaustion and grief are seen by God, and he offers real renewal.
entries.31:26: The prophet wakes from what felt like a sweet dream and sees it. It means God's promises can be so good they feel like a dream, and they give rest to the heart.
entries.31:27: God promises to fill Israel and Judah with people and animals like seed planted in a field. It means life and growth will return after emptiness.
entries.31:28: Just as God watched over them to tear down, he will now watch over them to build up and plant. It means God's purpose for his people has shifted from judgment to restoration.
entries.31:29: People will no longer quote the saying that parents eat sour grapes and children's teeth ache. It means the old complaint that you suffer for others' faults will no longer apply.
entries.31:30: Each person will bear the consequences of their own wrongdoing. It means responsibility is personal; you are not doomed by someone else's sin.
entries.31:31: God promises a coming day when he will make a new agreement with Israel and Judah. It means God is planning a fresh, deeper relationship with his people.
entries.31:32: The new agreement will not be like the old one that the people broke, even though God led them out of Egypt by the hand. It means the failure was on the people's side, and God is starting something better.
entries.31:33: God will put his law inside people and write it on their hearts, and he will be their God. It means following God will come from the inside, not just from rules on the outside.
entries.31:34: Everyone will know God directly, from the least to the greatest, and he will forgive their wrongdoing and remember their sin no more. It means knowing God becomes personal for all, and forgiveness is complete.
entries.31:35: God identifies himself as the one who set the sun, moon, and stars in place and stirs the sea. It means the God making these promises is the same one who holds the whole universe together.
entries.31:36: If the fixed order of the heavens could ever break, only then would Israel stop being a nation before God. It means God's commitment to his people is as stable as the created order.
entries.31:37: Only if the heavens could be measured and the earth's foundations searched out would God reject Israel for all they have done. It means God's faithfulness is not fragile, even when people fail.
entries.31:38: God promises a coming day when Jerusalem will be rebuilt, from one specific tower to a specific gate. It means restoration is concrete and planned, not vague.
entries.31:39: The measuring line will extend beyond the old boundaries to specific hills and around the city. It means God's rebuilding will expand beyond what people expect.
entries.31:40: Even the valley of dead bodies and the burial fields will become holy to the Lord, and the city will never be uprooted again. It means God can make the darkest, most defiled places holy and secure forever.
entries.32:1: This verse dates Jeremiah's message to a specific year, when Jerusalem was under threat. It reminds the reader that God's words come at real, datable moments in history.
entries.32:2: The Babylonian army had surrounded Jerusalem, and Jeremiah was locked up in a guarded courtyard. Even when God's messenger is confined, God's word is not.
entries.32:3: King Zedekiah had imprisoned Jeremiah for preaching that Babylon would capture the city. The reader sees that telling the truth can cost you your freedom.
entries.32:4: God said Zedekiah would not escape but would be captured and meet the Babylonian king face to face. What God announces will happen, however unlikely it seems.
entries.32:5: Zedekiah would be taken to Babylon and stay there until God showed mercy, and fighting Babylon would fail. Resisting what God has decreed brings no good outcome.
entries.32:6: Jeremiah introduces another message that came directly from God to him. God still speaks to his people in the middle of hard circumstances.
entries.32:7: God told Jeremiah in advance that his cousin would offer to sell him a field in Anathoth, which Jeremiah had the family right to buy. God knows and prepares what is coming.
entries.32:8: The cousin came exactly as God had said and offered the field, and Jeremiah recognized God's hand in it. When events match God's word, we can trust that he is at work.
entries.32:9: Jeremiah bought the field and paid the agreed price in silver. Faith sometimes shows itself in ordinary, costly actions.
entries.32:10: The sale was written down, sealed, witnessed, and the money weighed out. Jeremiah took care to make the deal legal and public, not secret.
entries.32:11: He kept both a sealed copy and an open copy of the deed. Careful records preserve what matters for the future.
entries.32:12: Jeremiah handed the deed to Baruch in front of his cousin, the witnesses, and everyone present. The purchase was done openly, with others able to confirm it.
entries.32:13: Jeremiah gave Baruch instructions in front of all the witnesses. Important actions were carried out with people watching and accountable.
entries.32:14: God told Jeremiah to put both copies of the deed in a clay jar so they would last a long time. God's promises are meant to be kept and trusted for the long haul.
entries.32:15: God promised that houses, fields, and vineyards would again be bought and sold in the land. Even while the city was doomed, God was promising future restoration.
entries.32:16: After handing over the deed, Jeremiah prayed to the Lord. Doing what God asks naturally leads us to talk with him.
entries.32:17: Jeremiah begins his prayer by praising God as creator, who made heaven and earth and can do anything. Nothing is too hard for the God we pray to.
entries.32:18: God shows mercy to thousands but also holds people accountable for sin that passes down through families. God is both kind and just, and he is called the Lord of armies.
entries.32:19: God is great in wisdom and mighty in action, watching everything people do and repaying each person for their conduct. Nothing we do is hidden from God.
entries.32:20: God performed signs and wonders in Egypt and has kept making his name known ever since. God's past acts show what he is still able to do.
entries.32:21: God brought Israel out of Egypt with signs, wonders, and great power, causing fear among the nations. God rescues his people in ways that are impossible to ignore.
entries.32:22: God gave Israel the land he had promised their ancestors, a land of plenty. God keeps the promises he made long ago.
entries.32:23: Israel took the land but disobeyed God and ignored his law, so disaster came on them. Blessing is tied to listening to God, and ignoring him brings trouble.
entries.32:24: The siege works were built, and the city was falling to Babylon by sword, famine, and disease, just as God had said. Jeremiah acknowledges that God's warning has come true.
entries.32:25: Jeremiah is puzzled: God told him to buy the field and have it witnessed, even though the city was about to fall to Babylon. Faithful obedience can leave us with questions we bring to God.
entries.32:26: God responds to Jeremiah's prayer with another message. God answers honest questions from those who trust him.
entries.32:27: God declares that he is Lord over all people and asks whether anything is too hard for him. No situation is beyond God's power.
entries.32:28: God confirms that he is handing the city over to Babylon and its king, who will capture it. What God has decided will certainly happen.
entries.32:29: The Babylonians would burn the city, including the roofs where people had worshiped false gods. The very places of idolatry would be destroyed.
entries.32:30: Israel and Judah had done evil since their earliest days, angering God with what they made and worshiped. Long-standing patterns of sin bring serious consequences.
entries.32:31: Jerusalem had provoked God's anger from its founding until that day, so he would remove it from his sight. Persistent sin eventually brings judgment.
entries.32:32: Everyone, from kings and officials to priests, prophets, and ordinary people, had joined in the evil that angered God. Sin was not limited to one group; the whole society shared in it.
entries.32:33: The people turned their backs on God and refused to listen, even though he taught them patiently again and again. Rejecting God's teaching is a serious matter.
entries.32:34: They placed their detestable idols in God's own temple and made it unclean. Treating what belongs to God as common dishonors him.
entries.32:35: They built shrines to Baal and sacrificed their children to Molech, things God never commanded and never intended. Such evil was so serious it led to Judah's removal from the land.
entries.32:36: God now speaks about the city that people said was doomed to Babylon by sword, famine, and disease. Even when judgment seems final, God is not finished speaking.
entries.32:37: God promises to gather his people back from all the countries where he scattered them and bring them home to live safely. Judgment is not the last word; God plans restoration.
entries.32:38: God promises that they will be his people and he will be their God. This is the heart of the relationship God restores.
entries.32:39: God promises to give them a united heart and a single path so they will worship him forever, for their good and their children's good. God himself changes people so they can stay faithful.
entries.32:40: God makes an everlasting covenant never to abandon them but always to do them good, and he puts reverence for him in their hearts so they will not turn away. God's commitment to his people is permanent and secure.
entries.32:41: God says he will genuinely enjoy doing good to his people and will commit himself fully to settling them securely in their land. For the reader, it means God's kindness is not reluctant but heartfelt, and he is personally invested in your good.
entries.32:42: God promises that just as he faithfully brought the disaster he warned about, he will now faithfully bring all the good he promised. For the reader, it means God's promises of good are as reliable as his warnings, so you can trust them.
entries.32:43: People will again buy and sell fields in the very land that seemed hopeless and abandoned to the enemy. For the reader, it means situations that look completely ruined are not beyond God's power to restore.
